projects.title: Unbaking the Sun
projects.tagline: Recovering the sun baked into photorealistic 3D city scans, and removing its shadows so the city can be relit.
projects.summary: Photogrammetric city meshes such as Google's Photorealistic 3D Tiles are frozen at one moment: the sun of capture day is painted into every texture. This project works out where that sun was from the mesh and texture alone, then removes its shadows so the city can be lit by any sun you choose.

stats.label: mean sun-direction error on clean synthetic cities
error with up to 1 m of vertex noise
candidate sun directions searched per tile
per tile on a laptop CPU, no GPU needed

sections.heading: The problem
body: Photorealistic 3D city scans are now everywhere in simulation, games and digital twins. Their textures are photographs, so every building carries the shadow it cast on capture day.
Put a new sun in the scene and you get two sets of shadows that disagree. Try it in the scene above: switch between Baked and Unbaked while the sun moves.
sections.caption: Baked aerial texture (left), ground-truth cast shadow (centre), and the shadow predicted from the recovered sun at 135.0°, 48.0° (right).

sections.heading: Finding the sun
body: For every texel of every texture atlas, the pipeline rasterises its 3D position and surface normal. For each candidate sun direction it ray-casts the whole scene to find which texels would be in shadow, then scores how well that explains the texture.

Fit measures how much of the texture's brightness a simple sun-plus-sky model explains. Edges checks whether brightness edges in the texture line up with predicted shadow edges: paint edges appear only in the texture, shadow edges in both. A coarse-to-fine search (5° → 1° → 0.25°) finds the peak.
sections.caption: Search score over every candidate azimuth and elevation. The edge test gives a sharp peak at the true sun.

sections.heading: Removing the shadows
body: With the sun known, the pipeline exports per-texel shadow masks, shading and ambient occlusion for every atlas. These give a geometry-only de-shadowed baseline today and condition a learned de-shadowing model next.
sections.caption: A synthetic tile's texture atlas: as captured with the baked sun, the computed shadow matte, and the unbaked result.

sections.heading: What validation shows
body:
• Clean geometry, five cities and five suns: mean error 0.07°, maximum 0.25°.
  • Vertices jittered by up to 1 m: still under 0.5°.
  • Rounded, blobby edges like real reconstructions: azimuth within about 5°, elevation biased about 8° low. Softened buildings cast shorter shadows, so the search lowers the sun to compensate. That mismatch is what the learned model has to absorb.
Next: paired synthetic training data, a conditioned de-shadowing network, and writing results back into 3D Tiles for Cesium for Unreal, starting with the Texas A&M campus.
sections.caption: Aerial render of a synthetic city with the geometric cast-shadow mask in red.

projects.title: Cold-Rolling Mill Digital Twin
projects.tagline: A digital twin that shows the hidden pressure inside a rolling mill, live, on the metal itself.
projects.credits: Faculty advisor / PI: Dr. Jian Tao
projects.summary: A physics-based digital twin of a robotic cold-rolling cell, built in NVIDIA Isaac Sim. Two UR10e arms feed an aluminum plate through a 3-D model of the lab's two-high mill. A roll-gap model computes the contact pressure and shows it as a live heat map in three places: in the gap, on a board above the mill, and painted onto the metal.

stats.label: Single-robot placements searched; none could serve both sides collision-free

sections.heading: Pressure no camera can see
body: Cold rolling squeezes metal between two steel rolls. The pressure that does the work acts on an arc only 6–8 mm long, hidden between the rolls. No camera or sensor can see it.

The twin computes that pressure at every step and draws it where it acts. In the white view every object turns translucent, the chock above the rolls is cut away, and only the metal stays solid, carrying its live heat map.
sections.caption: White view, pass 1. The plate enters the roll gap, and the part under the rolls shows its live contact pressure through the ghosted machine.

sections.heading: Physics plus a process model
body: PhysX runs at 240 Hz and handles everything rigid: the arms, the grippers, the powered roller tables, the sheet, and the wrist and finger-pad forces. But a rigid-body engine cannot deform metal.

At the bite, a roll-gap model takes over. It combines Bland–Ford theory with Hitchcock roll flattening, mill stretch and work hardening, then pulls the plate through the gap at its own entry and exit speeds. It outputs roll force, torque, power, forward slip, the new thickness and the full pressure curve along the arc.

Industrial mill twins split the work the same way: multibody physics for the handling, a reduced-order model for the pass. The predictions are not yet calibrated against the real mill. Expected uncertainty is ±10–20 %.
sections.caption: The validated three-pass schedule: (a) the friction hill along the arc of contact, (b) roll force and pressure per pass, (c) the pressure painted on each sheet, (d) roll force over the full schedule, with robot and mill activity.

sections.heading: Two robots, one direction
body: The lab's mill cannot be reached into or over. An offline search covered 968 single-robot placements beside the mill, with all eight arm configurations, and found no collision-free cycle that lets the sheet leave on the exit side. In the best case the upper arm still passed 4 mm into the handwheel rim.

So the cell uses two UR10e arms with Robotiq 2F-140 grippers. Robot A loads the plate and the mill rolls it. Robot B picks up the sheet at the exit and holds it up in front of the machine. Robot A takes the other end and turns it end for end on the way back to the entry table. The sheet only ever moves one way through the rolls.

Both arms stay at least 44 mm from the machine. One handling cycle takes about 60 s, and the full schedule runs in 183 s of simulated time with no collisions. Among the fixes: compliant, rubber-like pad contact cut how far a held sheet turned in the fingers from up to 17° to under 4°, and the sheet's collision body grows in 10 mm slices as the sheet lengthens.
sections.caption: The handover happens on the mill's drive side. Robot A stands on the left, robot B on the right.

sections.heading: The metal keeps a record
body: Each point on the sheet is painted with the peak pressure it felt in its last pass. The map moves with the metal along the exit table, through the handover and into the next pass.

The paint makes work hardening visible. As the plate goes from 6.0 to 3.6 mm, peak pressure climbs from 191 to 224 to 246 MPa, while roll force stays between 73.5 and 82.0 kN. The free head and tail stay 12–16 % lower.
A board above the mill shows the same live gap map, magnified about 80 times.
sections.caption: After pass 1, the rolled sheet waits at the exit end stop for robot B, painted with the pressure it felt.

sections.heading: Live in a browser
body: A web dashboard streams the real RTX render alongside every live quantity: thickness, roll force against capacity, pressure, torque, power, slip, temperature rise, the friction hill and the roll-bite geometry to scale. It has the same controls as the twin's own window and logs every pass to CSV and JSON.
The earlier one-robot version adds touchless control. In-browser MediaPipe hand tracking turns a webcam into a pointer: point to aim, pinch to click. The webcam image never leaves the browser.
Next comes the real mill: roll the same schedule, compare force, thickness and length, then calibrate friction and flow stress.
sections.caption: The dashboard during pass 1, over the live render. Controls sit on the left, gap pressure, friction hill and roll-bite geometry on the right, and live traces below.

gallery.caption: Robot A sets the plate on the powered entry table.
Real view of the mill's operator side. The yellow chock hides the roll bite, so the live gap map reads best in the white view and on the board.

projects.title: Yosemite National Park Digital Twin
projects.tagline: Yosemite in 3D, rebuilt from 6.87 billion laser points, with live weather, hazard maps and an AI guide.
projects.summary: A 3D digital twin of Yosemite that runs in a web browser. 202 km² are rebuilt from the USGS 2019 airborne LiDAR survey, and another 734 km² of USGS elevation data and aerial photos surround them. Visitors can follow live weather, open hazard maps, run a wildfire simulator, or ask an AI guide about the park.

stats.label: LiDAR points, USGS survey flown Oct 2019
Modeled: 202 km² in full 3D, 734 km² from USGS elevation

sections.heading: Billions of points, one surface
body: In October 2019, the USGS 3DEP program flew an airborne LiDAR survey over Yosemite. The twin starts from that raw data: 202 one-kilometre tiles and 6,867,935,812 laser points.

Each tile is cleaned, thinned and rebuilt as a continuous surface with Screened Poisson reconstruction in Open3D. Cliff points that were labeled as vegetation but behave like rock are relabeled as rock. A 25 m strip of points from the neighbouring tiles lets each tile meet the next without a seam.

The full-resolution meshes hold 682 million triangles, which is too many for a browser. So each tile streams in three levels of detail: a 3D mesh of about 400,000 triangles up close, then a 5 m grid and a 20 m grid farther away.
sections.caption: The Cathedral Range high country, looking northeast toward Tuolumne Meadows. Screenshot from the running twin.

sections.heading: Filling in the valley
body: The LiDAR tiles cover two areas: the north rim at the east end of Yosemite Valley, and the Tuolumne Meadows high country. Around and between them, another 734 km² comes from USGS 3DEP elevation data, almost all of it the 1 m model made from the same 2019 survey.
Every square kilometre is draped with the August 2022 NAIP aerial photo. On steep walls the color switches to granite tones, set by laser brightness in the LiDAR tiles.
Together the two cover everything from El Capitan and Half Dome to Clouds Rest and Tenaya Lake: 936 km² in one model.
sections.caption: El Capitan and Yosemite Valley, looking east toward Half Dome.

sections.heading: Every tree, counted
body: The trees come straight from the laser data. A 1 m map of canopy height marks every local high point 5 m or taller as a tree top. The twin holds more than 1.4 million trees, and the tallest detected so far measures 69.9 m.

Each tree is drawn at its measured height and colored from the aerial photo. The LiDAR does not record species, so they are inferred from the LANDFIRE vegetation map, the elevation and the tree's height.
A background job is now adding trees to the fill area from the same 2019 survey, one tile at a time.
sections.caption: Trees detected in the LiDAR near North Dome, with Half Dome behind.

sections.heading: Live data, simulated hazards
body: The twin follows the real park. Weather for Yosemite Valley and Tuolumne Meadows updates every 10 minutes and drives haze, rain and snow in the view. The sun is where it really is in the sky. Snow on the ground comes from NOAA SNODAS, Sentinel-2 and California snow sensors.
Hazard layers map rockfall zones with the shadow-angle method, rate wildfire hazard, and mark open, level ground where a helicopter could land.

A wildfire simulator spreads fire across 30 m cells using Rothermel's model and the 40 Scott & Burgan fuel models, with crown fire and embers added. You can draw fire lines or drop retardant and compare the outcome. It is an educational model, not an operational forecast.
sections.caption: Wildfire simulator: an escaped campfire near Half Dome, 8 simulated hours after ignition.

sections.heading: Ask, and it flies you there
body: An AI guide built on the Claude API answers typed or spoken questions about the park. It replies aloud with captions, flies the camera to the place in question, and switches map layers or weather to show what it means.
It works from the twin's own data: landmarks, trails, points of interest, the current weather and what the visitor is looking at.
Visitors are offered a narrated flight over the park, about 90 seconds long, before they explore on their own.

gallery.caption: Rockfall hazard over the east end of Yosemite Valley: cliffs steeper than 55° and the ground that falling blocks can reach.

projects.title: Phytoplankton — Swarm
projects.tagline: An interactive installation: hundreds of luminous plankton that come apart in your hands, and a pinch that brings one up close.
projects.summary: Hundreds of phytoplankton drift through a volume of dark water, each drawn from thousands of points of light. Raise a hand toward the camera and the plankton nearest it unravel into flowing pigment; the closer the hand, the wider and deeper the dissolve. Pinch one and the camera glides in to tell its story.

stats.label: plankton in the water by default, up to 600
particles simulated on the GPU every frame
species, each grown in 4 procedural variants
hands tracked at once from a single webcam

sections.heading: Reach into the water
body: The piece watches visitors through a webcam. MediaPipe hand tracking finds up to four hands, and the size of each palm in the frame tells how close it is to the wall.

As a hand approaches, the plankton nearest it come apart in organic patches, from the outside in, and drift away as coloured pigment. Pull back and the particles find their way home. A plankton that dissolved completely re-forms as a different species, always the one the swarm has least of, so the crowd stays diverse.
sections.caption: The swarm at rest. A live X / Y / Z readout floats beside every plankton as it wanders.

sections.heading: Pinch to look closer
body: Point at a plankton and touch thumb to index finger. A ring fills while the pinch is held; after half a second the camera glides in until the plankton fills much of the screen, and the rest of the swarm sinks into dark bokeh.

Up close, the same individual is redrawn from 65,536 points instead of 4,096, grown from the same seed so its cell counts and spines match. A panel gives its name, classification, size, habitat, a short description and a fact, along with its live position and the parameters it was grown from.
With no camera, a mouse or touchscreen does the same: click to look closer, press and hold to dissolve.
sections.caption: Close-up of Arachnoidiscus ehrenbergii, the 'spider-like disc', with its information panel.

sections.heading: Light, not meshes
body: Every plankton is a point cloud with a material per point: silica, rim or chloroplast. The look borrows from dark-field and fluorescence microscopy, where glass seen edge-on glows and chloroplasts carry their own colour.

Twenty species are generated procedurally, from diatoms such as Coscinodiscus, Chaetoceros and Asterionella to dinoflagellates such as the bioluminescent Pyrocystis and the red-tide alga Karenia brevis, coccolithophores, and colonies such as Volvox.
All 80 individuals live in one GPU texture, so changing a plankton's species is a single write while its particles are airborne. The new form simply condenses out of the cloud.
sections.caption: Gallery view: one of every species in the library.

sections.heading: The water sounds
body: Soft glassy voices swell as a hand nears the plankton, pitched by species and placed where each one is. Dissolving plankton fizz with bubbles, and re-forming ones ring like glass, over a quiet underwater drone.
Everything is synthesised live in the browser. There are no audio files.

sections.heading: Built for a gallery wall
body: The installation runs entirely in the browser on WebGL2 and works offline once set up. A launcher rebuilds it, serves it locally and opens Chrome full-screen in kiosk mode with the camera pre-approved.

It is made to run unattended. If the camera is unplugged it restarts and falls back to another camera; if the hand tracker fails it is rebuilt; if the GPU driver resets the page reloads. Hand detection runs on a background thread, and quality steps down by itself on slower machines.

sections.heading: Try it here
body: Run the installation in this page with your mouse: click a plankton to look closer, press and hold to dissolve. For hand tracking, open the full installation and allow the camera.
